idh.reasoning: The patient's age of 58 years is more typical for IDH-wildtype gliomas. The tumor's deep, midline location involving the thalamus, corpus callosum, and brain-stem, along with ependymal invasion and crossing the midline, is highly characteristic of IDH-wildtype glioblastoma. Furthermore, the presence of marked, thick-rim enhancement and a significant necrotic core are classic imaging features of IDH-wildtype tumors. The sharp tumor boundary, reflected in the thin FLAIR transition zone and high boundary sharpness score, also favors an IDH-wildtype status over the more diffusely infiltrating pattern of IDH-mutant astrocytomas. The absence of a T2-FLAIR mismatch sign argues against an IDH-mutant astrocytoma. There are no significant features to suggest an IDH-mutant tumor.

Moreover, the presence of marked, thick-rim enhancement and a large necrotic core is highly atypical for oligodendrogliomas, even anaplastic (Grade 3) ones. These aggressive features are much more characteristic of an astrocytic lineage tumor. Therefore, the evidence strongly supports a non-codeleted status.

The aggressive, infiltrative nature of the tumor, evidenced by deep white matter invasion, ependymal invasion, and crossing of the corpus callosum, also supports the highest grade. overall_comment: The combination of patient age (58 years) and MRI features—including a large, midline-crossing tumor with deep gray matter involvement, marked thick-rim enhancement, and extensive central necrosis—provides a classic presentation for Glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype, CNS WHO Grade 4.
